body:
in Online Courses, Uncategorized, Yale |   	November 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Taught by his­to­ri­an Mar­ci Shore, “Euro­pean Intel­lec­tu­al His­to­ry Since Niet­zsche” sur­veys the sto­ry of mod­ern thought, from the late 18th cen­tu­ry to the late 20th.
Along the way, the course explores major trends in mod­ern Euro­pean thought: Marx­ism-Lenin­ism, psy­cho­analy­sis, expres­sion­ism, struc­tural­ism, phe­nom­e­nol­o­gy, exis­ten­tial­ism, anti-pol­i­tics, and decon­struc­tion. Intel­lec­tu­al fig­ures cov­ered in the course include Niet­zsche, Lenin, Kaf­ka, Freud, Husserl, de Beau­voir, Hei­deg­ger, Arendt, Adorno, Sartre, Girard, Fou­cault, Der­ri­da, and Hav­el.
You can watch all 25 lec­tures above. Or find them on YouTube and Apple Pod­casts. Explore the course hand­outs here.
“Euro­pean Intel­lec­tu­al His­to­ry Since Niet­zsche” will be added to our col­lec­tion, 1,700 Free Online Cours­es from Top Uni­ver­si­ties.
If you would like to sup­port the mis­sion of Open Cul­ture, con­sid­er mak­ing a dona­tion to our site. It’s hard to rely 100% on ads, and your con­tri­bu­tions will help us con­tin­ue pro­vid­ing the best free cul­tur­al and edu­ca­tion­al mate­ri­als to learn­ers every­where. You can con­tribute through Pay­Pal, Patre­on, and Ven­mo (@openculture). Thanks!

title: When Animals Were Put on Trial in Medieval Europe
description:
in History, Law |   	November 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment

body:
in History, Law |   	November 13th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Most of us twen­ty-first-cen­tu­ry urban­ites have a fair­ly sen­ti­men­tal view of farm ani­mals, pre­cise­ly because so many gen­er­a­tions have gone by since they’ve been part of our dai­ly lives. (In South Korea, where I live, the agri­cul­tur­al past remains just with­in liv­ing mem­o­ry. Per­haps that’s why so many restau­rants in Seoul adver­tise their meat with pic­tures of the ani­mals it comes from, some­times dressed in chef’s garb and cheer­ful­ly serv­ing up the very dish­es they’re about to become.) Things were dif­fer­ent in medieval Europe, where ani­mals were both a neces­si­ty and a poten­tial dan­ger. His­to­ry records many instances of seri­ous harm done to humans by hors­es, bulls, and espe­cial­ly pigs, who seem to have had a par­tic­u­lar ten­den­cy to turn on chil­dren.
Today we would describe the killing of a child as an inhu­man act, a term that, in these cas­es, applies more than fig­u­ra­tive­ly. As for the fate of the vio­lent­ly offend­ing ani­mal, we might imag­ine that it would be sum­mar­i­ly slaugh­tered, but between the tenth and eigh­teenth cen­turies — and espe­cial­ly in the fif­teenth and six­teenth cen­turies — it might well have been brought into a court­room first. Though oth­er crea­tures had already been sub­ject to legal pro­ceed­ings for quite some time, “the ear­li­est record­ed pig tri­al took place in Fonte­nay-aux-Ros­es, just out­side Paris, in 1266,” writes Alexan­der Lee at His­to­ry Today. “By the ear­ly fif­teenth cen­tu­ry, how­ev­er, they had become estab­lished prac­tice through­out Nor­mandy and the Île-de-France,” even­tu­al­ly spread­ing beyond the bor­der to Italy, Ger­many, and the Low Coun­tries.
“As con­tem­po­rary stu­dents of the Cor­pus iuris civilis knew, it was a basic prin­ci­ple of Roman law that ani­mals could not be cul­pa­ble,” Lee adds. “Lack­ing rea­son, they were inca­pable of har­bor­ing crim­i­nal intent and hence could not be guilty of a crime.” But in un-Roman north­ern France, “the admin­is­tra­tion of sec­u­lar jus­tice was still large­ly the con­cern of local seigneurs and was gov­erned pre­dom­i­nant­ly by cus­tom rather than statute.” Thus sus­tained, ani­mal tri­als served pur­pos­es beyond sim­ple pun­ish­ment. “For medieval peo­ple, the world was cre­at­ed by God in a very log­i­cal way, with ani­mals cre­at­ed first, in order to serve and help human beings who were cre­at­ed in the image of God,” says Uni­ver­si­ty of Liv­er­pool medieval Euro­pean mon­ster expert Dami­an Kempf, quot­ed in Pop­u­lar Sci­ence by Anne Ewbank. In that world­view, try­ing and exe­cut­ing a pig could “restore what was bro­ken.”
Unlike domes­tic ani­mals, accord­ing to Sonya Vatom­sky at JSTOR Dai­ly, destruc­tive mice, bee­tles, snails, wee­vils, and oth­er ver­min would be sent to eccle­si­as­ti­cal tri­bunals. “Despite being unlike­ly can­di­dates for Catholi­cism, such crea­tures were pun­ished with excom­mu­ni­ca­tion, not exe­cu­tion,” she writes, since cast­ing them out of God’s domain would allow humans to exter­mi­nate them with peace of mind. Vatom­sky also quotes econ­o­mist Peter T. Leeson’s the­o­ry that the Catholic Church tried more ani­mals when peo­ple got lax about tithing, with the aim of “bol­ster­ing cit­i­zens’ belief in the valid­i­ty of Church pun­ish­ments for tithe eva­sion.” Putting ani­mals on tri­al may now strike us as grotesque, but like any alien-seem­ing episode of his­to­ry, it also reveals the beliefs on which a past soci­ety oper­at­ed — a mode of analy­sis that gets one won­der­ing how far the mod­ern Unit­ed States is from giv­ing them the right to sue.

title: When Salvador Dali Met Sigmund Freud, and Changed Freud’s Mind About Surrealism (1938)
description: The close asso­ci­a­tions between Sur­re­al­ism and Freudi­an psy­cho­analy­sis were lib­er­al­ly encour­aged by the most famous pro­po­nent of t
body:
The close asso­ci­a­tions between Sur­re­al­ism and Freudi­an psy­cho­analy­sis were lib­er­al­ly encour­aged by the most famous pro­po­nent of the move­ment, Sal­vador Dalí, who con­sid­ered him­self a devot­ed fol­low­er of Freud. We don’t have to won­der what the founder of psy­cho­analy­sis would have thought of his self-appoint­ed pro­tégé.
We have them record­ing, in their own words, their impres­sions of their one and only meeting—which took place in July of 1938, at Freud’s home in Lon­don. Freud was 82, Dalí 34. We also have sketch­es Dalí made of Freud while the two sat togeth­er. Their mem­o­ries of events, shall we say, dif­fer con­sid­er­ably, or at least they seemed total­ly bewil­dered by each oth­er. (Freud pro­nounced Dalí a “fanat­ic.”)
In any case, there’s absolute­ly no way the encounter could have lived up to Dalí’s expec­ta­tions, as the Freud Muse­um Lon­don notes:
[Dalí] had already trav­elled to Vien­na sev­er­al times but failed to make an intro­duc­tion. Instead, he wrote in his auto­bi­og­ra­phy, he spent his time hav­ing “long and exhaus­tive imag­i­nary con­ver­sa­tions” with his hero, at one point fan­ta­siz­ing that he “came home with me and stayed all night cling­ing to the cur­tains of my room in the Hotel Sach­er.” 
Freud was cer­tain­ly not going to indulge Dalí’s pecu­liar fan­tasies, but what the artist real­ly want­ed was val­i­da­tion of his work—and maybe his very being. “Dalí had spent his teens and ear­ly twen­ties read­ing Freud’s works on the uncon­scious,” writes Paul Gal­lagher at Dan­ger­ous Minds, “on sex­u­al­i­ty and The Inter­pre­ta­tion of Dreams.” He was obsessed. Final­ly meet­ing Freud in ’38, he must have felt “like a believ­er might feel when com­ing face-to-face with God.”

He brought with him his lat­est paint­ing The Meta­mor­pho­sis of Nar­cis­sus, and an arti­cle he had pub­lished on para­noia. This, espe­cial­ly, Dalí hoped would gain the respect of the elder­ly Freud.
Try­ing to inter­est him, I explained that it was not a sur­re­al­ist diver­sion, but was real­ly an ambi­tious­ly sci­en­tif­ic arti­cle, and I repeat­ed the title, point­ing to it at the same time with my fin­ger. Before his imper­turbable indif­fer­ence, my voice became invol­un­tar­i­ly sharp­er and more insis­tent.
On being shown the paint­ing, Freud sup­pos­ed­ly said, “in clas­sic paint­ings I look for the uncon­scious, but in your paint­ings I look for the con­scious.” The com­ment stung, though Dalí wasn’t entire­ly sure what it meant. But he took it as fur­ther evi­dence that the meet­ing was a bust. Sketch­ing Freud in the draw­ing below, he wrote, “Freud’s cra­ni­um is a snail! His brain is in the form of a spiral—to be extract­ed with a nee­dle!”

One might see why Freud was sus­pi­cious of Sur­re­al­ists, “who have appar­ent­ly cho­sen me as their patron saint,” he wrote to Ste­fan Zweig, the mutu­al friend who intro­duced him to Dalí. In 1921, poet and Sur­re­al­ist man­i­festo writer André Bre­ton “had shown up unin­vit­ed on [Freud’s] doorstep.” Unhap­py with his recep­tion, Bre­ton pub­lished a “bit­ter attack,” call­ing Freud an “old man with­out ele­gance” and lat­er accused Freud of pla­gia­riz­ing him.
Despite the mem­o­ry of this nas­ti­ness, and Freud’s gen­er­al dis­taste for mod­ern art, he could­n’t help but be impressed with Dalí. “Until then,” he wrote to Zweig, “I was inclined to look upon the sur­re­al­ists… as absolute (let us say 95 per­cent, like alco­hol), cranks. That young Spaniard, how­ev­er, with his can­did and fanat­i­cal eyes, and his unde­ni­able tech­ni­cal mas­tery, has made me recon­sid­er my opin­ion.”
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2020.

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

title: 2,800-Year-Old Bone Flute Unearthed in Troy May Have Been Played During Homer’s Time
description:
in Archaeology, History |   	November 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twit­ter
The pro­lif­ic Hans Zim­mer scored
body:
in Archaeology, History |   	November 12th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
Image by Mehmet Nuri Ersoy, via Twit­ter
The pro­lif­ic Hans Zim­mer scored Christo­pher Nolan’s films over the dozen years from Bat­man Begins through Dunkirk. From 2020’s Tenet onward, Nolan has employed the younger Swedish com­pos­er Lud­wig Görans­son. Just what dif­fer­ence this has made in the result­ing pic­tures is a mat­ter best left to the scruti­ny of the most obses­sive fans, but any view­er can hear how much Zim­mer and Görans­son dif­fer styl­is­ti­cal­ly. This past sum­mer, the siren song includ­ed on the sound­track of The Odyssey fea­tured one of the lat­ter’s par­tic­u­lar­ly notable choic­es: the use of an aulos, a dou­ble-reed­ed wind instru­ment much played back in ancient Greece.
Though Görans­son did­n’t have a gen­uine­ly ancient aulos on hand, of course, the sound pro­duced by the repli­ca proved evoca­tive enough. But just this year, as it hap­pens, a bone flute actu­al­ly dat­ing from the peri­od in which Homer wrote The Odyssey was unearthed from the archae­o­log­i­cal site of ancient Troy in mod­ern-day north­west­ern Turkey.
As Smithsonian.com’s Meilan Sol­ly writes, the past 160 years of dig­ging there have pro­duced “a pair of gold diadems, more than 100 two-han­dled wine gob­lets, and arrow­heads and weapons dat­ed to the Late Bronze Age, among oth­er arti­facts.” This 2,800-year-old flute isn’t just the first musi­cal instru­ment dis­cov­ered at the site, but also fur­ther evi­dence that Troy was­n’t the ghost town it was once assumed to be in the eighth cen­tu­ry BC.

As always when deal­ing with ancient arti­facts — and espe­cial­ly ones, as these pic­tures reveal, in a less-than-whole state — we should be care­ful with our terms. “Call­ing the object a flute is the exca­va­tors’ choice of word, and the type remains open,” says Ancient Ori­gins. While this new dis­cov­ery could poten­tial­ly be a real Greek aulos, “with­out hole counts or a pub­lished draw­ing, match­ing the Troy find to that design is pre­ma­ture.” Archae­ol­o­gists have unearthed sim­i­lar instru­ments else­where, dat­ing from dif­fer­ent peri­ods, but nev­er before has one emerged from the buried remains of a city so rich in leg­endary asso­ci­a­tions. To those in search of a deep­er under­stand­ing of antiq­ui­ty, the site con­tin­ues to sound a siren song of its own.

title: Seán Doran's 'Crimson Star' Tours the Raging Surface of the Sun
description: Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The footage-li
body:
Celestial filmmaker Seán Doran is back with a new project that interprets stellar snapshots from NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory. The footage-like video tours the sun and reveals its fiery surface complete with brilliant solar flares, all depicted in a distinctive crimson.
To create the film, Doran attributed various pinks and reds to different wavelengths, creating an alluring interpretation of the fiery orb. Doran stitched together NASA’s captures, or more accurately, he says, the images were “conformed, repaired, graded, blended, rescaled and retimed” into a seamless film. “Crimson Star” is one of several astral projects he’s undertaken in recent years, and you can keep up with his latest works on YouTube. (via Kottke)

title: Get Up-Close to Cells, Ink, and Insects in the Nikon Small World Photomicrography Contest
description: From fungi and insects to technology and crystals, the winning entries in the 2026 Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition reveal astonishi
body:
From fungi and insects to technology and crystals, the winning entries in the 2026 Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition reveal astonishing details typically invisible to the naked eye. This year’s top prize went to Ole Bielfeldt, a student and experimental photographer based in Cologne, Germany, who used a hand-built rig to capture an incredible up-close view of droplets inside of an inkjet printer. Runners-up included John-Oliver Dum’s portrait of a jumping spider with pollen on its body and Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery’s capture of mouse neurons.
Winner images were organized into three categories: Top 20, Honorable Mentions, and Images of Distinction. Explore some of our favorites here, and head to the contest’s website to see all of this year’s best photos. You might also enjoy the Nikon Small World in Motion video competition.
1st Place: Ole Bielfeldt (Cologne, Northrhine-Westfalia, Germany). Microscopic view of an inkjet printer depositing ink onto paper
3rd Place: Kaelin Wulf and Ms. Rachel Flannery (Allen Institute, Department of Neural Dynamics, Seattle, Washington, U.S.). Neurons in an expanded mouse brain
Image of Distinction: Charles Krebs (Issaquah,  Washington, U.S.). Tardigrade (“Water Bear”) clearly showing the piercing stylets and pharnyx used to eat
6th Place: Eric Epstein (Brooklyn, New York, U.S.). Hemitrichia slime mold spore structures (fruiting bodies)
9th Place: Dr. Francisco Lázaro-Diéguez (Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Bronx, New York, U.S.) Dedifferentiated liver endothelial cell
14th Place: Mike Crutchley (Pembrokeshire, Southwest Wales, U.K.). Pilobolus fungi on sheep dung
15th Place: Dr. Julien Resseguier (University of Oslo, Department of Biosciences, Oslo, Viken, Norway). Mouse trachea showing tiny hair-like cells that move mucus and nearby nerves (blue) associated with the muscles (yellow)
Image of Distinction: Giuseppe Franchina (Messina, Italy). Western honey bee (Apis mellifera) with pollen
Image of Distinction: Sergey Kichigin (Vologda, Russia). A snowflake under a microscope
Honorable Mention: Jan Martinek (Czech Academy of Sciences, Institute of Experimental Botany, Prague, Czech Republic). A common daisy flower head (Bellis perennis) glowing with its natural autofluorescence

title: 'The Sacred Ordinary' Shines a Light on Heritage in Birmingham's Civil Rights District
description: In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated pl
body:
In the second stanza of “How to Be a Poet,” Wendell Berry wrote: “There are no unsacred places; / there are only sacred places / and desecrated places.” When it comes to preserving important historical locations, such as monuments, parks, and buildings, a new interactive public art installation asks, “what happens when preservation itself is endangered?”
The Sacred Ordinary is an initiative organized by 1504, a production studio based in Birmingham that emphasizes in-depth storytelling to connect people with meaningful, human-focused services and experiences. The participatory artwork is presented in collaboration with the National Parks Conservation Association, which aims to protect U.S. national parks for future generations.

In early 2025, President Trump issued an executive order that mandated the removal of some National Park Service signage relating to slavery, the LGBTQ+ community, climate change, and more, a move that erases histories inextricable from the nation’s identity. (The current administration has also blocked millions in funding for numerous parks and disrupted services.)
In Birmingham, the Civil Rights District is formally designated a national monument, comprising neighborhoods that Black people historically called home and where Jim Crow laws authorized segregation until the 1960s. The Civil Rights Movement reached a nexus here when activists Fred Shuttlesworth, Martin Luther King, Jr., and Ralph Abernathy, among many others, organized nonviolent marches in 1963, known today as the Birmingham Campaign. Police turned their dogs on demonstrators and used fire hoses on children. A bombing at a Baptist church killed four young Black girls.
The Sacred Ordinary venerates access to things most of us take for granted: the ability to shop at any store, attend the nearest school, walk around any neighborhood, and sit at the front of the bus. The exhibition is installed around-the-clock, but by day, elements of the installation comprise vintage yet mundane objects that one typically walks by without giving a second thought.
A huge midcentury television rests on an open lawn, and a red newspaper vending box for The Birmingham News, which ceased its print publication in 2012, advertises 25 cents per copy. Additional sites include a characteristically blue U.S. Postal Service mailbox and a walk-in telephone booth. Sheets of paper with tear-off tabs posted around town invite participants to learn more by texting a phone number. If you text “HERE” to the number, you’ll be directed to a starting point and an otherwise nondescript yellow fire hydrant.

In scavenger-hunt style, visitors are prompted to enter the year stamped on the unit, and if it’s between 5 and 8 p.m., the sequence of texted prompts doubles as a multimedia self-guided tour of Birmingham’s Civil Rights District like you’ve never seen it: the television screen, mailbox, phone booth, and more begin to glow once the sun has set. 
“Birmingham, Alabama, is known around the world for such places—sites of civil rights history that many regard as sacred and that connect us to something larger than ourselves. But today, that memory is endangered,” 1504 says in a statement. “Aging infrastructure, the passing of a generation of foot soldiers, and federal efforts to erase chapters of American history raise an urgent question: if institutions alone cannot sustain history, what role can the public play in caring for sacred sites?”
Rather than center primarily on signage, The Sacred Ordinary focuses on objects associated with civic life in the mid-20th century, evoking collective memories and providing touchpoints for younger generations for whom boxy televisions, printed newspapers, and telephone booths feel distant from today’s experiences. Emblematic of the way news and information spread before the internet and smartphones, the objects confront visitors with not only the realities of how people organized and communicated during that time but also how those memories are preserved today. Even without didactics, objects and places carry meaning that no one can simply delete.
The tour opens with a narration by actor André Holland, who played a fundamental role in preserving a historic theater in nearby Bessemer, Alabama, and 1504 has dedicated the installation to Birmingham-based artist Joe Minter. The Sacred Ordinary continues nightly through December 13, with accompanying guided walks and other programs scheduled in the meantime. Learn more on the project’s website, and explore the studio’s work on Instagram. You might also be interested in “The Praise House,” directed by 1504’s Tyler Jones.
